Learning Objectives
Define energy availability and understand the risks of inadequate energy availability.
Specify macronutrients and understand the general recommended intake amounts and timing
for adequate fueling in athletes.
Specify micronutrients and understand the general recommended intake amounts and if
supplementation is necessary.
Define supplements and understand the advantages and dosing of legal supplements and the
risks of illegal supplements.

Training and nutrition are periodized.
The macronutrient ratios and amount of energy via nutrition required vary based on the
amount and intensity of training and recovery occurring on a short-term (ie, day to day) and
long-term (ie, months) basis.
The goals of nutrition for training differ from those for competition.1
Energy availability is an important foundation.
Energy availability is the amount of energy available to the body to perform all other
functions after the cost of exercise is subtracted.
Chronically low energy availability is associated with multifaceted system dysfunctions,
including but not limited to reproductive, gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, endocrine, and
musculoskeletal systems (relative energy deficiency syndrome).
Typically, athletes with an energy availability of less than 30 kcal/kg fat-free mass have a
greater risk of experiencing multiple system dysfunction.
Adequate energy availability is defined as 45 kcal/kg fat-free mass.2
Main sources of energy from food
Glycogen: a storage product of carbohydrates (CHOs)
Fat: a main source for prolonged low-intensity exercise via fatty acid oxidation
Protein: a source only if glycogen stores are depleted during prolonged exercise (eg,
ultramarathon Resource 1)
Macronutrients
Nutrients and timing of intake are key components of sports nutrition.
CHO
Primary source of energy for exercising muscles
Overall recommended CHO intake: 3 to 12 g/kg
Light (low intensity): 3 to 5 g/kg per day
Moderate (1-hour training per day): 5 to 7 g/kg per day
High (1 to 3 hours of moderate/high-intensity training per day): 6 to 10 g/kg per day
Very high (4 to 5 hours of moderate/high-intensity training per day): 8 to 12 g/kg per
day1
Timing for peak performance
1 to 4 hours before exercise: 1 to 4 g/kg for exercise longer than 60 minutes
During exercise (>60 minutes): 30 to 60 g/hr, up to 90 g/hr if ultra-endurance exercise

Can also use oral CHO rinse for exercise lasting 45 to 75 minutes
Optimal percentage of CHO solution for liquids: 6% to 8% (eg, 15 g CHO per 240 mL)
After exercise: 1.0 to 1.2 g/hr for first 4 hours
Vital if recovery period is less than 8 hours1
Fat
Overall recommended intake: 1 to 3 g/kg
Most athletes, along with the general public, are encouraged to follow the Dietary Guidelines
for Americans: 20% to 30% of total caloric intake
Very low-fat diets (<20%) are detrimental to performance and do not lead to additional
weight loss when restricting calories.3
High-fat diets with low CHO intake
Studies show enhancing rates of fat oxidation in endurance athletes
Likely no impact on performance for moderate-intensity exercise
Concern regarding decreased performance in sprint/high-intensity exercises
Secondary to low blood glucose levels and limited glycogen availability4
Protein
Ideal to have a variety of high-quality plant and animal-based protein in diet
On average, athletes require approximately double the amount of protein compared with a
sedentary adult.
Protein made up of amino acids: nine total essential amino acids
Three essential amino acids absorbed fastest: leucine, isoleucine, and valine
Multiple studies link leucine to muscle protein synthesis4
Recommended protein intake
Endurance athletes: 1.2 to 1.4 g/kg per day
Team sports: 1.2 to 1.7 g/kg per day
Strength: 1.6 to 1.7 g/kg per day
Power: 1.5 to 1.7 g/kg per day
Per meal: 0.25 to 0.30 g/kg
Approximately 20 g per meal is adequate for most athletes1,5,6
Fluids and electrolytes
Hydration is vital to training and performance, with a rule of thumb being that for every
pound lost during exercise, 2 to 3 cups (0.48 to 0.72 L) of fluid should be consumed.
American College of Sports Medicine fluid and electrolyte recommendations
Fluid loss greater than 2% total body weight may lead to decreased performance

Methods for monitoring fluid status
Measure weight before and after exercise
Monitor urine color and/or specific gravity
Monitor symptoms of thirst
Calculate sweat rate (pre-exercise weight - post-exercise weight) + (fluid intake - urine
volume)/length of exercise in hours7
Micronutrients
Athletes can meet overall requirements for vitamins and minerals with nutrient-dense and
fortified foods in diet alone.
Athletes in weight-restricted sports and lean sports (eg, distance runners, gymnasts) are at
higher risk for deficiencies.
Vitamins and minerals
Iron: iron deficiency with or without anemia may limit work capacity
Higher risk of deficiency: females, low-calorie diets, distance runners because of foot strike
hemolysis
Supplementation
If true anemia is present, 3 to 6 months typically necessary to normalize levels
Studies suggest mild performance improvement in management of iron deficiency
without anemia
Caution regarding over-supplementation: gastrointestinal distress and iatrogenic
hemochromatosis4
Vitamin D
Essential fat-soluble vitamin important in bone metabolism
Estimated 90% derived from skin exposure to ultraviolet sunlight
Moderate amount of evidence shows deficiency correlated with increased upper-
respiratory infections
Supplementation
Recommended daily allowance: 400 to 800 IU/d
Reduction in stress fracture risk: 800 IU to 1,000 IU/d1
Calcium
Important for many systems, including muscle function, vascular system, and bone
metabolism

Supplementation
Recommended daily allowance:1,000 to 1,300 mg/d
Known low energy availability or female athlete triad: 1,500 mg/d1
Supplements
Dietary supplements must be evaluated based on safety, efficacy, and legality (cost-benefit
ratio).
Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994
Each company is responsible for testing for safety and appropriate labeling.8
US Food and Drug Administration is not authorized or responsible for reviewing dietary
supplements for safety and effectiveness before they are marketed
Legal Supplements
Creatine
Creatine is one of the most popular nutritional supplements, derived from the amino acids
glycine, arginine, and methionine.
Most creatine is stored in muscle. In its phosphorylated form, creatine contributes to the
resynthesis of adenosine triphosphate.
Studies on creatine loading in high-intensity performance show an increase in isometric
strength (<150 seconds) and improvements in lean mass and in strength and power with
maintenance supplementation.
Short-term adverse effect for acute loading phase: 1- to 2-kg increase in body mass because of
water retention
Long-term adverse effects: no known adverse effects from using creatine supplements for as
long as 4 years, but longer-term studies have not been conducted
Dosing
Loading dose: 20 g/d divided into four doses for 5 to 7 days
Maintenance dose: 3 to 5 g/d9
Caffeine
Consumed daily by athletes and nonathletes throughout the world, caffeine can be used to
enhance athletic performance.

Doses as low as 2 to 3 mg/kg have been documented to improve performance.
The mechanism of action is adenosine receptor antagonist. Caffeine is thought to improve
performance by increasing endorphin release, increasing alertness, improving neuromuscular
function, and reducing the perception of exertion.
Dosing
3 to 6 mg/kg of body mass 60 minutes before performance in anhydrous form (pill or
powder)
Less than 3 mg/kg during performance, with CHO
No performance benefit of more than 9 mg/kg
Athletes must exercise caution in using caffeine. Dietary intake in combination with an
unknown amount of caffeine in supplements (because of lack of regulation) may lead to an
unexpected positive test result.
Adverse effects: tachycardia, nausea, anxiety, tremors9
Caffeine is no longer banned by the International Olympic Committee, the World Anti-Doping
Agency, or the National Collegiate Athletic Association,10 but its use is monitored, and
restrictions or penalties may be applied if urine concentrations are greater than 12 μg/mL for
the International Olympic Committee and greater than 15 μg/mL for the National Collegiate
Athletic Association.
Nitrate
Enhances nitric oxide availability, and mechanism of sports performance enhancement
includes improved skeletal muscle contraction and improved muscle blood flow.
Studies show small improvement in performance (0.3% to 3%) during events lasting only 30
seconds to 10 minutes
Dosing
Daily dosing: 65 mg/kg body mass via split doses three to four times per day for 10 to 12
weeks9
Illegal Supplements
Anabolic Steroids
Anabolic steroids are believed to be widely abused in athletes of all ages, with use reported in
as many as 10% of adolescent athletes.

Adverse effects include atherosclerotic disease, decreased high-density lipoprotein cholesterol
levels, aggression and mood disturbances, testicular atrophy, masculinization in females,
gynecomastia in males, acne, and an increased risk of hepatitis and HIV infections in athletes
sharing needles to inject steroids.
Most adverse effects are believed to be reversible with cessation of use; however, a prolonged
period may be required to return to normal levels.
Most organizations test for anabolic steroids, looking for a testosterone to epitestosterone
ratio higher than 6:1.
Erythropoietin
Erythropoietin acts to stimulate hemoglobin production, which, increases the body’s oxygen-
carrying capacity.
This ability has made erythropoietin widely desirable among elite endurance athletes.
Several studies have documented increases in hematocrit levels and the maximum volume of
oxygen consumption in time to exhaustion.
Adverse effects of erythropoietin use include stroke, thromboembolic events, and myocardial
infarctions resulting from increased blood viscosity.
Human Growth Hormone
Human growth hormone is a peptide secreted by the anterior pituitary gland that stimulates
the release of insulin-like growth factors.
Studies have been conducted in patients with endocrine dysfunction; results showed increases
in muscle size but not in strength.
Adverse effects include water retention, myopathy, carpal tunnel syndrome, and insulin
resistance.
